title: The fifth through ninth arguments: transmitted indications
en:
Fifth: his saying, God bless him and grant him peace, “Follow the two who come after me: Abū Bakr and ʿUmar.” Sixth: his saying, “The caliphate after me will last thirty years; then it will become biting kingship”—that is, the subjects will suffer injustice at the rulers’ hands, as though the latter were biting them. Abū Bakr’s caliphate lasted two years, ʿUmar’s ten, ʿUthmān’s twelve, and ʿAlī’s six.
Seventh: during the illness in which he died, he said, “Bring me writing materials and a sheet, so that I may write a document for Abū Bakr about which no two persons will disagree”; then he said, “God and the Muslims will accept none but Abū Bakr.” Eighth: the Emigrants whom God described as “those who are truthful” used to address him as “Successor of the Messenger of God.”
Ninth: the Prophet appointed him to lead the prayers, which are the foundation of the Law, and did not dismiss him. The report of dismissal is a fabrication of the Rāfiḍa. Hence, when Abū Bakr said, “Release me, for I am not the best of you,” he—may God be pleased with him—said: “We shall neither release you nor seek to be released from you. The Messenger of God put you forward, so none should put you back. He approved you for our religion, and we have approved you for our worldly affairs.”
ar: الخامس قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم اقتدوا باللذين من بعدي أبي بكر وعمر السادس قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم الخلافة من بعدي ثلاثون سنة ثم تصير ملكا عضوضا أي ينال الرعية منهم ظلم كأنهم يعضون عضا وكانت خلافة أبي بكر سنتين وخلافة عمر عشر سنين وخلافة عثمان اثنتي عشرة سنة وخلافة علي ست سنين السابع قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم في مرضه الذي توفي فيه ائتوني بكتاب وقرطاس أكتب لأبي بكر كتابا لا يختلف فيه اثنان ثم قال يأبى الله والمسلمون إلا أبا بكر الثامن أن المهاجرين الذين وصفهم الله بقوله أولئك هم الصادقون كانوا يقولون له يا خليفة رسول الله التاسع أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم استخلفه في الصلوات التي هي أساس الشريعة ولم يعزله ورواية العزل افتراء من الروافض ولهذا لما قال أبو بكر أقيلوني فلست بخيركم قال رضي الله عنه لا نقيلك ولا نستقيلك قدمك رسول الله فلا يؤخرك رضيك لديننا فرضيناك لدنيانا

title: The tenth argument and the evidential force of the set
en: Tenth: if the imamate had belonged by right to ʿAlī, Abū Bakr had usurped it, and the community had approved this and supported him rather than ʿAlī, they would not have been the best community brought forth for humanity, commanding right and forbidding wrong. The consequent is false. Although these arguments yield probability, the appointment of an imam belongs to practical matters, for which probability suffices. Moreover, taken together they may yield certainty for some impartial persons. Even conceding otherwise, they are at least suitable as a supporting basis and confirmation of the consensus.
ar: العاشر لو كانت الإمامة حقا لعلي غصبها أبو بكر ورضيت الجماعة بذلك وقاموا بنصرته دون علي رضي الله عنه لما كانوا خير أمة أخرجت للناس يأمرون بالمعروف وينهون عن المنكر واللازم باطل وهذه الوجوه وإن كانت ظنيات فنصب الإمام من العمليات فيكفي فيه الظن على أنها باجتماعها ربما تفيد القطع لبعض المنصفين ولو سلم فلا أقل من صلوحها سندا للإجماع وتأييدا

title: Introduction to the Shīʿī arguments and a polemical digression
en:
He says: the Shīʿa have advanced several arguments. In establishing ʿAlī’s imamate after the Prophet, they appeal to reason, transmission, and criticism of those other Companions of the Messenger of God who assumed the office. They claim recurrent transmission for many reports in this discussion, relying upon their fame among themselves, their frequent repetition on their tongues and in their assemblies, their conformity with their dispositions, and their constant arrival at their ears. They do not reflect upon how these could have remained unknown to the eminent Anṣār and Emigrants and to trustworthy transmitters and traditionists; why some did not invoke them against others, nor base their decisions and reversals upon them; or why they appeared only after the age of the imamate had passed, the prophetic mission had become remote, cold partisanships and corrupt contrivances had arisen, and religious affairs had fallen to evil scholars and government to unjust rulers.
Among the astonishing things is that some later Shīʿī partisans, who had neither met any traditionist nor transmitted a report concerning religion, filled their books with such reports and attacks upon the excellent Companions. Consider the book al-Tajrīd attributed to the philosopher Naṣīr al-Ṭūsī: how it supports falsehoods and establishes lies. Yet the great members of the Prophet’s household and the descendants of the Legatee, distinguished by understanding and protected in transmission, did not harbour these grudges and partisanships. They mentioned only the Companions’ excellences and treated the leaders of the schools among the scholars of Islam only with reverence and esteem.
ar: قال احتجت الشيعة بوجوه لهم في إثبات إمامة علي رضي الله عنه بعد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وجوه من العقل والنقل والقدح فيمن عداه من أصحاب رسول الله الذين قاموا بالأمر ويدعون في كثير من الأخبار الواردة في هذا الباب التواتر بناء على شهرته فيما بينهم وكثرة دورانه على ألسنتهم وجريانه في أنديتهم وموافقته لطباعهم ومقارعته لأسماعهم ولا يتأملون أنه كيف خفي على الكبار من الأنصار والمهاجرين والثقاة من الرواة والمحدثين ولم يحتج به البعض على البعض ولم يبنوا عليه الإبرام والنقض ولم يظهر إلا بعد انقضاء دور الإمامة وطول العهد بأمر الرسالة وظهور التعصبات الباردة والتعسفات الفاسدة وإفضاء أمر الدين إلى علماء السوء والملك إلى أمراء الجور ومن العجائب أن بعض المتأخرين من المتشيعين الذين لم يروا أحدا من المحدثين ولا رووا حديثا في أمر الدين ملأوا كتبهم من أمثال هذه الأخبار والمطاعن في الصحابة الأخيار وإن شئت فانظر في كتاب التجريد المنسوب إلى الحكيم نصير الطوسي كيف نصر الأباطيل وقرر الأكاذيب والعظماء من عترة النبي وأولاد الوصي الموسومون بالدراية المعصومون في الرواية لم يكن معهم هذه الأحقاد والتعصبات ولم يذكروا من الصحابة إلا الكمالات ولم يسلكوا مع رؤساءالمذاهب من علماء الإسلام إلا طريق الإجلال والإعظام

section: 45 · Investigation V: the succession and the first four caliphs
unit_notes: Tawātur is translated “recurrent transmission” here: transmission on a scale taken to preclude collusion on a falsehood. Al-waṣī, “the Legatee,” is the designation of ʿAlī in this passage. The denunciation of Ṭūsī and the characterisation of Shīʿī transmission are preserved as authorial polemic, not endorsed as independent findings.
en_html: He says: the Shīʿa have advanced several arguments. In establishing ʿAlī’s imamate after the Prophet, they appeal to reason, transmission, and criticism of those other Companions of the Messenger of God who assumed the office. They claim recurrent transmission for many reports in this discussion, relying upon their fame among themselves, their frequent repetition on their tongues and in their assemblies, their conformity with their dispositions, and their constant arrival at their ears. They do not reflect upon how these could have remained unknown to the eminent Anṣār and Emigrants and to trustworthy transmitters and traditionists; why some did not invoke them against others, nor base their decisions and reversals upon them; or why they appeared only after the age of the imamate had passed, the prophetic mission had become remote, cold partisanships and corrupt contrivances had arisen, and religious affairs had fallen to evil scholars and government to unjust rulers. Among the astonishing things is that some later Shīʿī partisans, who had neither met any traditionist nor transmitted a report concerning religion, filled their books with such reports and attacks upon the excellent Companions. Consider the book al-Tajrīd attributed to the philosopher Naṣīr al-Ṭūsī: how it supports falsehoods and establishes lies. Yet the great members of the Prophet’s household and the descendants of the Legatee, distinguished by understanding and protected in transmission, did not harbour these grudges and partisanships. They mentioned only the Companions’ excellences and treated the leaders of the schools among the scholars of Islam only with reverence and esteem.

title: The alleged succession document of al-Riḍā
en: Here is the imam ʿAlī b. Mūsā al-Riḍā: despite his lofty standing, renowned name, perfect learning and guidance, scrupulousness and piety, he wrote on the reverse of al-Maʾmūn’s document designating him as successor words indicating abundant praise, acceptance of the designation, and commitment to its conditions—even though at its conclusion he wrote, “Al-Jāmiʿa and … indicate the contrary.” He also prayed for God’s good pleasure upon al-Maʾmūn. Between the lines of the designation, beneath “I have named him al-Riḍā,” he wrote, “May God be pleased with you and make you pleased”; beneath “He shall hold the supreme command after me,” he wrote, “Rather, may I be your ransom”; and elsewhere, “You have maintained the bond of kinship and have been recompensed with good.” This document, in their two hands, is now present at the Riḍā shrine in Khurāsān. Yet individual Shīʿīs in this age will not invoke God’s good pleasure upon the eminent Companions, much less upon the ʿAbbāsids: let them at least accept like for like.
ar: وها هو الإمام علي بن موسى الرضي مع جلالة قدره ونباهة ذكره وكمال علمه وهداه وورعه وتقواه قد كتب على ظهر كتاب عهد المأمون له ما ينبئ عن وفور حمده وقبول عهده والتزام ما شرط عليه وإن كتب في آخره والجامعة و . . . يدلان على ضد ذلك ثم أنه دعا للمأمون بالرضوان فكتب في أثناء أسطر العهد تحت قوله وسميته لرضي رضي الله عنك وأرضاك وتحت قوله ويكون له الإمرة الكبرى بعدي بل جعلت فداك وفي موضع آخر وصيتك رحم وجزيت خيرا وهذا العهد بخطهما موجود الآن في المشهد الرضوي بخراسان وآحاد الشيعة في هذا الزمان لا يسمون الكبار الصحابة بالرضوان فضلا عن بني العباس فقد رضوا رأسا برأس

title: A grant attributed to ʿUmar and its alleged confirmation by ʿAlī
en: Another clear and evident instance in this matter is what the Commander of the Faithful, ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, wrote: “I have assigned to the family of Banū Kākula, as a charge upon the Muslims’ treasury, two hundred mithqāls of coined, pure gold every year. Written by Ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.” The Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī, then wrote: “To God belongs the command before and after, and on that day the believers will rejoice. I am the first to follow the command of him who strengthened Islam and supported religion and its rulings, ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb. I have ordered the same as he ordered for the family of Banū Kākula: two hundred dinars of coined, pure gold every year. I have followed his example and assigned to them the same as ʿUmar ordered, since following that is incumbent upon me and all Muslims. Written by ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib.” This, in their two hands, is now present in the lands of Iraq.
ar: ومن البين الواضح في هذا الباب ما كتبه أمير المؤمنين عمر بن الخطاب فقد جعلت لآل بني كاكلة على كافة بيت المسلمين كل عام مائتي مثقال ذهبا عينا إبريزا كتبه ابن الخطاب فكتب أمير المؤمنين علي رضي الله عنه لله الأمر من قبل ومن بعد ويومئذ يفرح المؤمنون أنا أول من اتبع أمر من أعز الإسلام ونصر الدين والأحكام عمر بن الخطاب ورسمت بمثل ما رسم لآل بني كاكلة في كل عام مائتي دينار ذهبا عينا إبريزا واتبعت أثره وجعلت لهم بمثل ما رسم عمر إذ وجب علي وعلى جميع المسلمين اتباع ذلك كتبه علي بن أبي طالب وهذا بخطهما موجود الآن في ديار العراق

title: The rational argument for ʿAlī and the reply
en:
He says: first. This is the rational argument. Its formulation is that there is no dispute that there must be an imam after the Messenger; that imam can be none other than ʿAlī, because the imam must be infallible, designated by an authoritative text, and the best person of his age. None of these properties is found in the other Companions. The absence of infallibility and designation is agreed; the absence of superiority will be established below. This may be made into three arguments, corresponding to the three conditions. Sometimes it is presented by turning the argument around: the imam is either ʿAlī, Abū Bakr, or al-ʿAbbās, by a consensus which includes the infallible imam’s statement; the last two possibilities are excluded because the condition is absent.
The reply is, first, to deny that these conditions are required, and second, to deny that the conditions are absent from Abū Bakr. As for the claim that consensus that the imam is one of these men amounts to consensus that each is eligible for the imamate, that is open to examination.
ar: قال الأول هذا هو الوجه العقلي وتقريره أنه لا نزاع في أن بعد الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم إماما وليس غير علي لإن الإمام يجب أن يكون معصوما ومنصوصا عليه وأفضل أهل زمانه ولا يوجد شيء من ذلك في باقي الصحابة أما العصمة والنص فبالاتفاق وأما الأفضلية فلما سيأتي وهذا يمكن أن يجعل أدلة ثلاثة بحسب الشروط وربما يورد في صورة القلب فيقال الإمام إما علي رضي الله عنه وإما أبو بكر وإما العباس بالإجماع المشتمل على قول المعصوم ولا سبيل إلى الأخيرين لانتفاء الشرط والجواب أولا منع الاشتراط وثانيا منع انتفاء الشرائط في أبي بكر رضي الله عنه وأما ما يقال أن الإجماع على أن الإمام أحدهم إجماع على صلوح كل منهم للإمامة فمحل نظر

section: 45 · Investigation V: the succession and the first four caliphs
unit_notes: Naṣṣ is an authoritative designation, not merely any reference in a text. The final qualification rejects a potentially invalid move from an exhaustive disjunction to each disjunct’s individual eligibility.
en_html: He says: first. This is the rational argument. Its formulation is that there is no dispute that there must be an imam after the Messenger; that imam can be none other than ʿAlī, because the imam must be infallible, designated by an authoritative text, and the best person of his age. None of these properties is found in the other Companions. The absence of infallibility and designation is agreed; the absence of superiority will be established below. This may be made into three arguments, corresponding to the three conditions. Sometimes it is presented by turning the argument around: the imam is either ʿAlī, Abū Bakr, or al-ʿAbbās, by a consensus which includes the infallible imam’s statement; the last two possibilities are excluded because the condition is absent. The reply is, first, to deny that these conditions are required, and second, to deny that the conditions are absent from Abū Bakr. As for the claim that consensus that the imam is one of these men amounts to consensus that each is eligible for the imamate, that is open to examination.

title: The verse of walāya: the argument
en:
He says: second. This refers to the transmitted argument from the Book. Its formulation is that the verse, “Your walī is only God, His Messenger, and those who believe, who establish prayer and give alms while bowing,” was revealed—by the commentators’ agreement—concerning ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib when he gave his ring to a petitioner while bowing in prayer. The particle innamā conveys restriction, as transmission and usage attest. Just as walī can mean a supporter, it can mean the one exercising authority, or the person with the prior and stronger right to it: one says that a woman’s brother is her walī, that the sovereign is the walī of one who has none, and that someone is the walī entitled to claim redress for bloodshed.
That is the intended meaning here. For walāya in the sense of support extends to all believers, as the Exalted says, “Believing men and believing women are supporters of one another.” It therefore cannot properly be restricted to believers described as establishing prayer and giving alms while bowing. The believer who exercises authority over the community’s affairs is the imam. Hence ʿAlī is determined for that office, since these descriptions were not found in anyone else.
ar: قال الثاني إشارة إلى الدليل النقلي من الكتاب وتقريره أن قوله تعالى إنما وليكم الله ورسوله والذين آمنوا الذين يقيمون الصلاة ويؤتون الزكاة وهم راكعون نزلت باتفاق المفسرين في علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله عنه حين أعطى السائل خاتمه وهو راكع في صلاته وكلمة إنما للحصر بشهادة النقل والاستعمال والولي كما جاء بمعنى الناصر فقد جاء بمعنى المتصرف والأولى والأحق بذلك يقال أخو المرأة وليها والسلطان ولي من لا ولي له وفلان ولي الدم وهذا هو المراد ههنا لأن الولاية بمعنى النصرة تعم جميع المؤمنين لقوله تعالى والمؤمنون والمؤمنات بعضهم أولياء فلا يصح حصرها في المؤمنين الموصوفين بإقامة الصلاة وإيتاء الزكاة حال الركوع والمتصرف من المؤمنين في أمر الأمة يكون هو الإمام فتعين علي رضي الله عنه لذلك إذ لم توجد هذه الصفات في غيره

title: The verse of walāya: contextual and grammatical replies
en:
The reply is to deny that walī here means one who administers religious and worldly affairs and has the superior right to do so, as is peculiar to the imam. Rather, it means supporter, ally, and …, in keeping with what precedes and follows the verse: “Believers, do not take Jews and Christians as allies; they are allies of one another.” Restriction establishes for one party what has been denied of another. The prohibited walāya toward Jews and Christians is not administration or the imamate, but support and affection. The same applies to “Whoever allies himself with God, His Messenger, and those who believe—God’s party are the victors,” and “Whoever among you allies himself with them belongs to them.” Evidently, this is a bond of affection and support, not an imamate.
In short, one who reflects on the verse’s context and knows the usages of speech will see that walī here does not entail the imamate but denotes alliance, support, and affection. The believers’ description may also be intended for praise and magnification rather than restriction and specification: to increase the honour of those described, their entitlement and priority to be taken as allies, their closeness, their support, and the compassion which moves them to support others. “While they are bowing” may be circumstantial, but may equally be a coordinated clause meaning that they bow in their prayers, unlike Jewish prayer which lacks bowing, or meaning that they are humble.
ar: والجواب منع كون الولي بمعنى المتصرف في أمر الدين والدنيا والأحق بذلك على ما هو خاصة الإمام بل الناصر والموالي و . . . على ما يناسب ما قبل الآية وما بعدها وهو قوله تعالى يا أيها الذين آمنوا لا تتخذوا اليهود والنصارى أولياء بعضهم أولياء بعض فإن الحصر إنما يكون بإثبات ما نفي عن الغير وولاية اليهود والنصارى المنهي عن اتخاذها ليست هي التصرف والإمامة بل النصرة والمحبة وقوله تعالى ومن يتول الله ورسوله والذين آمنوا فإن حزب الله هم الغالبون وقوله تعالى ومن يتولهم منكم فإنه منهم لظهور أن ذلك تولي محبة ونصرة لا إمامة وبالجملة لا يخفى على من تأمل في سياق الآية وكان له معرفة بأساليب الكلام أن ليس المراد بالولي ههنا ما يقتضي الإمامة بل الموالاة والنصرة والمحبة ثم وصف المؤمنين لما ذكر يجوز أن يكون للمدح والتعظيم دون التقييد والتخصيص وأن يكون لزيادة شرف الموصوفين واستحقاقهم أن يتخذوا أولياء وأولويتهم بذلك وقربهم ونصرتهم وشفقتهم الحاملة على النصرة وقوله وهم راكعون كما يحتمل الحال يحتمل العطف بمعنى أنهم يركعون في صلاتهم لا كصلاة اليهود خالية عن الركوع أو بمعنى أنهم خاضعون

title: Additional objections to the inference from walāya
en:
There are further objections. Support, although general, necessarily concerns those other than the particular group of believers to whom it is attributed, since a person does not support himself. It is as though some believers were told, “Your supporters are only the others.” Imām al-Rāzī says that this objection is the one to rely upon in repelling the difficulty, since it is subtle and sound. You will recognise, however, that it rests on the address being confined to some believers and the described believers comprising everyone else.
Another objection is that restriction denies an alternative about which hesitation or dispute has arisen. At the time of revelation, that alternative was plainly not the imamate of the first three imams. Again, the apparent sense establishes walāya actually and at the present time, whereas ʿAlī’s imamate was certainly after the Prophet. To say that he already possessed governing authority over the Muslims during the Prophet’s life is obstinacy; to make walāya refer to the future rather than the present does not work in the case of God and His Messenger.
Further, “those who believe” is plural and cannot be applied to a single person without evidence. The commentators’ statement that the verse was revealed concerning ʿAlī does not entail that its scope is exclusively his. The claim that the descriptions apply only to him depends on treating “while they are bowing” as a circumstantial clause modifying the pronoun in “they give”; this is not necessary. Finally, had the verse indicated ʿAlī’s imamate, that indication would not have remained unknown to the Companions generally or to ʿAlī specifically, and they would not have neglected to comply with it and invoke it.
ar: على أن ههنا وجوها أخر من الاعتراض منها أن النصرة وإن كانت عامة لكن إذا أضيفت إلى جماعة مخصوصة من المؤمنين فبالضرورة تختص بمن عداهم لأن الإنسان لا يكون ناصرا لنفسه وكأنه قيل لبعض المؤمنين إنما ناصركم البعض الآخر قال الإمام الرازي إن هذا السؤال عليه التعويل في دفع هذه الشبهة فإنه دقيق متين وأنت خبير بأن مبناه على اختصاص الخطاب بالبعض من المؤمنين وعلى كون المؤمنين الموصوفين جميع من عداهم ومنها أن الحصر إنما يكون نفيا لما وقع فيه تردد ونزاع ولا خفاء في أن ذلك عند نزول الآية لم يكن إمامة الأئمة الثلاثة ومنها أن ظاهر الآية ثبوت الولاية بالفعل وفي الحال ولا شبهة في أن إمامة علي رضي الله عنه إنما كانت بعد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم والقول بأنه كانت له ولاية التصرف في أمر المسلمين في حياة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أيضا مكابرة وصرف الولاية إلى ما يكون في المآل دون الحال لا يستقيم في حق الله تعالى ورسوله ومنها أن الذين آمنوا صيغة جمع فلا يصرف إلى الواحد إلا بدليل وقول المفسرين أن الآية نزلت في حق علي رضي الله عنه لا يقتضي اختصاصها به واقتصارها عليه ودعوى انحصار الأوصاف فيه مبنية على جعل وهم راكعون حالا من ضمير يؤتون وليس بلازم ومنها أنه لو كانت في الآية دلالة على إمامة علي رضي الله عنه لما خفيت على الصحابة عامة وعلى علي خاصة ولما تركوا الانقياد لها والاحتجاج بها

section: 45 · Investigation V: the succession and the first four caliphs
unit_notes: The reservation following the citation of al-Rāzī is Taftāzānī’s own qualification; it is not removed in translation.
en_html: There are further objections. Support, although general, necessarily concerns those other than the particular group of believers to whom it is attributed, since a person does not support himself. It is as though some believers were told, “Your supporters are only the others.” Imām al-Rāzī says that this objection is the one to rely upon in repelling the difficulty, since it is subtle and sound. You will recognise, however, that it rests on the address being confined to some believers and the described believers comprising everyone else. Another objection is that restriction denies an alternative about which hesitation or dispute has arisen. At the time of revelation, that alternative was plainly not the imamate of the first three imams. Again, the apparent sense establishes walāya actually and at the present time, whereas ʿAlī’s imamate was certainly after the Prophet. To say that he already possessed governing authority over the Muslims during the Prophet’s life is obstinacy; to make walāya refer to the future rather than the present does not work in the case of God and His Messenger. Further, “those who believe” is plural and cannot be applied to a single person without evidence. The commentators’ statement that the verse was revealed concerning ʿAlī does not entail that its scope is exclusively his. The claim that the descriptions apply only to him depends on treating “while they are bowing” as a circumstantial clause modifying the pronoun in “they give”; this is not necessary. Finally, had the verse indicated ʿAlī’s imamate, that indication would not have remained unknown to the Companions generally or to ʿAlī specifically, and they would not have neglected to comply with it and invoke it.

title: Ghadīr Khumm: the report and its key word
en:
He says: third. They appeal to reports which they claim to have been recurrently transmitted. As for the report of Ghadīr, it states that he, peace be upon him, gathered the people on the day of Ghadīr Khumm, a place between Mecca and Medina at al-Juḥfa, on his return from the Farewell Pilgrimage. It was a summer day, so hot that a man would put his cloak under his feet. Saddles were gathered, and he mounted them and addressed the people: “Community of Muslims, do I not have a greater claim over you than you have over yourselves?” They said, “Indeed, by God!” He said, “Whoever has me as his mawlā has ʿAlī as his mawlā. God, befriend whoever befriends him, be the enemy of whoever is his enemy, support whoever supports him, and forsake whoever forsakes him.”
This report’s authenticity is agreed, they say: ʿAlī cited it on the day of the consultation when setting out his merits, and no one denied it. Mawlā may mean the manumitter, the freed person, the confederate, the neighbour, the cousin, the supporter, or the person with the prior right of disposal. The Exalted says, “Your abode is the Fire: it is your mawlā”—that is, most entitled to you, as Abū ʿUbayda explained. And the Prophet said, “Any woman who marries herself without her mawlā’s permission”—that is, the one with the greater claim concerning her and authority to manage her affairs. Similar usage is frequent in poetry.
ar: قال الثالث تمسك بما يدعون فيه التواتر من الأخبار أما حديث الغدير فهو أنه عليه السلام قد جمع الناس يوم غدير خم موضع بين مكة والمدينة بالحجفة وذلك بعد رجوعه عن حجة الوداع وكان يوما صائفا حتى أن الرجل ليضع رداءه تحت قدميه من شدة الحر وجمع الرجال وصعد عليه السلام عليها وقال مخاطبا معاشر المسلمين ألست أولى بكم من أنفسكم قالوا اللهم بلى قال فمن كنت مولاه فعلى مولاه اللهم وال من والاه وعاد من عاداه وانصر من نصره واخذل من خذله وهذا حديث متفق على صحته أورده علي رضي الله عنه يوم الشورى عندما حاول ذكر فضائله ولم ينكره أحد ولفظ المولى قد يراد به المعتق والمعتق والحليف والجار وابن العم والناصر والأولى بالتصرف قال الله تعالى مأواكم النار هي مولاكم أي أولى بكم ذكره أبو عبيدة وقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أيما امرأة نكحت نفسها بغير إذن مولاها أي الأولى بها والمالك لتدبير أمرها ومثله في الشعر كثير

title: Why the opponent takes mawlā to denote authority
en: In sum, the use of mawlā for the holder and master of an office and the person with the prior right to exercise authority is common in Arabic and reported from many leading lexicographers. The point is that it is a noun for this meaning, not an adjective equivalent in form to awlā, so that one could object that it is not an elative and is not used as one. This meaning should be intended in the report, to correspond to its opening. There is evidently no basis for the first five meanings, nor for the sixth, since mutual support is already obvious and needs neither explanation nor the gathering of people—especially when God has said, “Believing men and believing women are supporters of one another.” It is evident that authority over people, administration, and mastery over the management and disposition of their affairs in the Prophet’s manner constitute the meaning of the imamate.
ar: وبالجملة استعمال المولى بمعنى المتولي والمالك للأمر والأولى بالتصرف شائع في كلام العرب منقول عن كثير من أئمة اللغة والمراد أنه اسم لهذا المعنى لا صفة بمنزلة الأولى ليعترض بأنه ليس من صيغة اسم التفضيل وأنه لا يستعمل استعماله وينبغي أن يكون المراد به في الحديث هو هذا المعنى ليطابق صدر الحديث ولأنه لا وجه للخمسة الأول وهو ظاهر ولا للسادس لظهوره وعدم احتياجه إلى البيان وجمع الناس لأجله سيما وقد قال الله تعالى والمؤمنون والمؤمنات بعضهم أولياء بعض ولا خفاء في أن الولاية بالناس والتولي والمالكية لتدبير أمرهم والتصرف فيهم بمنزلة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم هو معنى الإمامة

title: The reply to the argument from Ghadīr
en:
The reply is to deny the report’s recurrent transmission: this is one of the Shīʿa’s obstinate claims. How could it be otherwise when many traditionists criticised its authenticity, and exacting authorities among them—such as al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and al-Wāqidī—did not transmit it? Most of those who transmitted it did not transmit the introductory statement made the proof that mawlā means “the one with the prior right.” Even supposing the narration sound, its ending, “God, befriend whoever befriends him,” suggests that mawlā means supporter and beloved friend. Indeed, the mere possibility of that meaning suffices to defeat the inference.
The observation that such support is already known from “Believing men and believing women are supporters of one another” does not exclude the possibility. The purpose may have been to make explicit his entitlement to allegiance and support, placing it further beyond the specification to which most general statements are subject, strengthening the indication and conveying greater honour through its conjunction with allegiance to the Prophet. That degree of affection and support does not establish the imamate. Even granting an indication of the imamate, a solitary report has no weight against consensus. Even granting that, it shows at most entitlement to the imamate and its future establishment; how does the negation of the imamate of his predecessors follow? This is a concession of what the evidence entails, and it is an evident reply which the disputants have not mentioned.
On reflection, their alleged recurrent transmission is an argument against them, not for them. Had the report been intended to establish and indicate the imamate, it would not have remained obscure to the eminent Companions: they would not have failed to invoke it or hesitated about the office. To say that the people refused compliance out of obstinacy and that ʿAlī refrained from invoking it through protective concealment is a sign of error and the height of impudence.
ar: والجواب منع تواتر الخبر فإن ذلك من مكابرات الشيعة كيف وقد قدح في صحته كثير من أهل الحديث ولم ينقله المحققون منهم كالبخاري ومسلم والواقدي وأكثر من رواه لم يرو المقدمة التي جعلت دليلا على أن المراد بالمولى الأولى وبعد صحة الرواية فمؤخر الخبر أعني قوله اللهم وال من والاه يشعر بأن المراد بالمولى هو الناصر والمحب بل مجرد احتمال ذلك كاف في دفع الاستدلال وما ذكره من أن ذلك معلوم ظاهر من قوله تعالى والمؤمنون والمؤمنات بعضهم أولياء بعض لا يدفع الاحتمال لجواز أن يكون الغرض التنصيص على موالاته ونصرته ليكون أبعد عن التخصيص الذي تحتمله أكثر العمومات وليكون اقوى دلالة وأوفى بإفادة زيادة الشرف حيث قرن بموالاة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وهذا القدر من المحبة والنصرة لا يقتضي ثبوت الإمامة وبعد تسليم الدلالة على الإمامة فلا عبرة بخبر الواحد في مقابلة الإجماع ولو سلم فغايته الدلالة على استحقاق الإمامة وثبوتها في المال لكن من اين يلزم نفي إمامة الأئمة قبله وهذا قول بالموجب وهو جواب ظاهر لم يذكره القوم وإذا تأملت فما يدعون من تواتر الخبر حجة عليهم لا لهم لأنه لو كان مسوقا لثبوت الإمامة دالا عليه لما خفي على عظماء الصحابة فلم يتركوا الاستدلال به ولم يتوقفوا في أمرالإمامة والقول بأن القوم تركوا الانقياد عنادا وعلي رضي الله تعالى عنه ترك الاحتجاج تقية آية الغواية وغاية الوقاحة

section: 45 · Investigation V: the succession and the first four caliphs
unit_notes: Qawl bi-l-mūjab means conceding the evidence’s actual implication while denying that it proves the disputed conclusion. The author distinguishes authenticity, recurrent transmission, semantics, and chronological priority. His negative claims concerning transmitters require a separate ḥadīth audit. «في المال» is read as «في المآل», “eventually/in the future.”
en_html: The reply is to deny the report’s recurrent transmission: this is one of the Shīʿa’s obstinate claims. How could it be otherwise when many traditionists criticised its authenticity, and exacting authorities among them—such as al-Bukhārī, Muslim, and al-Wāqidī—did not transmit it? Most of those who transmitted it did not transmit the introductory statement made the proof that mawlā means “the one with the prior right.” Even supposing the narration sound, its ending, “God, befriend whoever befriends him,” suggests that mawlā means supporter and beloved friend. Indeed, the mere possibility of that meaning suffices to defeat the inference. The observation that such support is already known from “Believing men and believing women are supporters of one another” does not exclude the possibility. The purpose may have been to make explicit his entitlement to allegiance and support, placing it further beyond the specification to which most general statements are subject, strengthening the indication and conveying greater honour through its conjunction with allegiance to the Prophet. That degree of affection and support does not establish the imamate. Even granting an indication of the imamate, a solitary report has no weight against consensus. Even granting that, it shows at most entitlement to the imamate and its future establishment; how does the negation of the imamate of his predecessors follow? This is a concession of what the evidence entails, and it is an evident reply which the disputants have not mentioned. On reflection, their alleged recurrent transmission is an argument against them, not for them. Had the report been intended to establish and indicate the imamate, it would not have remained obscure to the eminent Companions: they would not have failed to invoke it or hesitated about the office. To say that the people refused compliance out of obstinacy and that ʿAlī refrained from invoking it through protective concealment is a sign of error and the height of impudence.

title: The report of Aaron’s position: argument and principal replies
en:
As for the report of the position, it is his saying to ʿAlī: “You stand to me in the position of Aaron to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me.” Their argument is that “position” is a generic noun in a construct phrase, and so has general scope, as when made definite by the article; the possibility of an exception proves this. Once the prophetic rank is excepted, the expression remains general over the other positions, including being Moses’ successor, administrator of affairs, disposer of the public interest, and an obligatorily obeyed leader had he survived him. For it would not be fitting to the prophetic rank that this exalted position, established during Moses’ life, should disappear upon his death. Since prophethood is explicitly excluded, this can be only by way of the imamate.
The reply is to deny recurrent transmission: rather, it is a solitary report opposed to consensus. We also deny the generality of the positions. At most, a singular noun annexed to a proper name is unrestricted; it may even denote a particular known relation, as in “Zayd’s servant.” The stated exception does not exclude an individual instance of “position,” as would “except prophethood”; it is a disconnected exception meaning “but,” as is plain to those who know Arabic, and therefore proves no generality. Moreover, blood-brotherhood was among Aaron’s positions, and was not established for ʿAlī—unless it be said that this is effectively excepted because its absence is obvious. Even granting generality, deputyship and the exercise of authority by delegation, as implied by the imamate, were not among Aaron’s positions, since he shared prophethood with Moses. “Take my place” is not an appointment to succession but an emphatic instruction to undertake the people’s affairs.
ar: وأما حديث المنزلة فهو قوله عليه السلام لعلي رضي الله تعالى عنه أنت مني بمنزلة هارون من موسى إلا أنه لا نبي بعدي وتقريره أن المنزلة اسم جنس ضعيف فعم كما إذا عرف باللام بدليل صحة الاستثناء وإذا استثنى منها مرتبة النبوة بقيت عامة في باقي المنازل التي من جملتها كونه خليفة له ومتوليا في تدبير الأمر ومتصرفا في مصالح العامة ورئيسا مفترض الطاعة لو عاش بعده إذ لا يليق بمرتبة النبوة زوال هذه المرتبة الرفيعة الثابتة في حياة موسى عليه السلام بوفاته وإذ قد صرح بنفي النبوة لم يكن ذلك إلا بطريق الإمامة والجواب منع التواتر بل هو خبر واحد في مقابلة الإجماع ومنع عموم المنازل بل غاية الاسم المفرد المضاف إلى العلم الإطلاق وربما يدعى كونه معهودا معينا كغلام زيد وليس الاستثناء المذكور إخراجا لبعض أفراد المنزلة بمنزلة قولك إلا النبوة بل منقطع بمعنى لكن على ما لا يخفى على أهل العربية فلا يدل على العموم كيف ومن منازله الأخوة في النسب ولم يثبت لعلي اللهم إلا أن يقال أنها بمنزلة المستثنى لظهور انتفائها ولو سلم العموم فليس من منازل هارون الخلافة والتصرف بطريق النيابة على ما هو مقتضى إلإمامة لأنه شريك له في النبوة وقوله اخلفني ليس استخلافا بل مبالغة وتأكيدا في القيام بأمرالقوم

title: Further replies and the limitation of the Tabūk answer
en:
Even granting that, nothing indicates that the position persists after death. Its ending with the death of the one who delegated it is neither dismissal nor diminution; it may instead be a return to a more complete condition, namely independence in prophethood and in conveying from God. Even granting persistence, Aaron’s exercise of authority and the efficacy of his command, had he remained after Moses, would have been due to his prophethood. Prophethood is absent in ʿAlī’s case, so what is founded upon and results from it is absent as well.
As for the answer that, when the Prophet left for the Tabūk expedition, he put ʿAlī in charge of Medina, whereupon the hypocrites spoke much about it and ʿAlī asked, “Messenger of God, are you leaving me with those left behind?” He replied, “Are you not content to stand to me as Aaron stood to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me?” It is argued that this does not establish succession after his death, just as Ibn Umm Maktūm was placed in charge of Medina during many expeditions. But this answer may be rejected on the ground that consideration is given to the generality of the wording, not the particular occasion. Indeed, it may be argued that putting him in charge of Medina without later dismissing him, together with the absence of any recognised distinction between the cases and the stronger need for a successor after death than during absence, indicates that he is the successor.
ar: ولو سلم فلا دلالة على بقائها بعد الموت وليس انتفاؤها بموت المستخلف عزلا ولا نقصا بل ربما يكون عودا إلى حالة أكمل هي الاستقلال بالنبوة والتبليغ من الله تعالى ولو سلم فتصرف هارون عليه السلام ونفاذ أمره لو بقي بعد موسى إنما يكون لنبوته وقد انتفت النبوة في حق علي رضي الله تعالى فينتفي ما يبتنى عليها ويتسبب عنها وأما الجواب بأن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم لما خرج إلى غزوة تبوك استخلف عليا على المدينة فأكثر أهل النفاق في ذلك فقال علي يا رسول الله أتتركني مع الاختلاف فقال صلى الله عليه وسلم أما ترضى أن تكون مني بمنزلة هارون من موسى إلا أنه لا نبي بعدي وهذا لا يدل خلافته بعده كابن أم مكتوم رضي الله تعالى عنه استخلفه على المدينة في كثير من غزواته فربما يدفع بأن العبرة لعموم اللفظ لا لخصوص السبب بل ربما يحتج بأن استخلافه على المدينة وعدم عزله عنها مع أنه لا قائل بالفصل وأن الاحتياج إلى الخليفة بعد الوفاة أشد وأوكد منه حال الغيبة يدل على كونه خليفة

section: 45 · Investigation V: the succession and the first four caliphs
unit_notes: «مع الاختلاف» is anomalous; “those left behind” is a provisional reading of an expected form such as al-khawālif, explicitly flagged. The final sentences are the author’s acknowledgement of a rejoinder against one Sunni reply, not his own unqualified conclusion in favour of designation.
en_html: Even granting that, nothing indicates that the position persists after death. Its ending with the death of the one who delegated it is neither dismissal nor diminution; it may instead be a return to a more complete condition, namely independence in prophethood and in conveying from God. Even granting persistence, Aaron’s exercise of authority and the efficacy of his command, had he remained after Moses, would have been due to his prophethood. Prophethood is absent in ʿAlī’s case, so what is founded upon and results from it is absent as well. As for the answer that, when the Prophet left for the Tabūk expedition, he put ʿAlī in charge of Medina, whereupon the hypocrites spoke much about it and ʿAlī asked, “Messenger of God, are you leaving me with those left behind?” He replied, “Are you not content to stand to me as Aaron stood to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me?” It is argued that this does not establish succession after his death, just as Ibn Umm Maktūm was placed in charge of Medina during many expeditions. But this answer may be rejected on the ground that consideration is given to the generality of the wording, not the particular occasion. Indeed, it may be argued that putting him in charge of Medina without later dismissing him, together with the absence of any recognised distinction between the cases and the stronger need for a successor after death than during absence, indicates that he is the successor.

title: Reports of explicit designation
en:
He says: fourth. These are reports which they claim are explicit prophetic designations of ʿAlī as successor: his address to the Companions, “Greet him with the title Commander of the Faithful”—the pronoun refers to ʿAlī; imra, with kasra, means command, from amira, “to become a commander.” Also: “You are the successor after me”; “He is the imam of the God-fearing and leader of those with radiant faces and limbs”; his taking ʿAlī’s hand and saying, “This is my successor over you”; and his saying to ʿAlī, “You are my brother, my legatee, my successor after me, and the discharger of my debt.”
The reply is what preceded: they are solitary reports opposed to consensus; had they been sound, they would not have remained unknown to the Companions, Successors, and skilled, scrupulous traditionists, especially his pure descendants. Even granting them, their utmost implication is to establish his succession, not to negate the succession of the others.
ar: قال الرابع هذه أخبار يدعون أنها نصوص جلية من النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم على خلافة علي رضي الله تعالى عنه وهو قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم مخاطبا لأصحابه سلموا عليه يإمرة المؤمنين الضمير لعلي والإمرة بالكسر الإمارة من أمر الرجل صار أميرا وقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام لعلي رضي الله تعالى عنه أنت الخليفة من بعدي وقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام أنه أمام المتقين وقائد الغر المحجلين وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم وقد أخذ بيد علي هذا خليفتي عليكم وقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام لعلي رضي الله تعالى عنه أنت أخي ووصيي وخليفتي من بعدي وقاضي ديني بالكسر والجواب ما مر أنها أخبار آحاد في مقابلة الإجماع وأنها لو صحت لما خفيت على الصحابة والتابعين والمهرة المتقين من المحدثين سيما على أولاده الطاهرين ولو سلم فغايته إثبات خلافته لا نفي خلافة الآخرين

title: Disqualification arguments and prophetic inheritance
en:
He says: fifth. This argues for ʿAlī’s imamate by attacking the imamate of the others. There is no dispute that an imam exists after the Prophet, and none of those so designated other than ʿAlī is eligible. In general, this is because they were wrongdoers owing to their previous unbelief: “The unbelievers are the wrongdoers”; and a wrongdoer cannot be imam, because “My covenant does not embrace the wrongdoers.” The reply denies both premises, denies that the verse classifies someone who once disbelieved and then embraced Islam as a wrongdoer, and denies that “covenant” here means the imamate.
In detail, one criticism of Abū Bakr is that he opposed God’s Book by denying inheritance from the Prophet on the basis of a report which he himself transmitted: “We, the company of prophets, leave no inheritance; what we leave is charity.” The Book, they say, may be specified only by a recurrently transmitted report, not by a solitary one. The reply is that a solitary report, though probable in its textual transmission, may be certain in its indication. It may therefore specify a general statement of the Book, which is probable in indication even though certain in textual transmission, thereby reconciling the two proofs. The full investigation belongs to legal theory. Moreover, a report heard from the Messenger’s own mouth is, if not above a recurrently transmitted report, plainly equal to it. A qualified jurist who heard it may therefore specify a general statement of the Book by it.
ar: قال الخامس استدلال على إمامة علي رضي الله تعالى عنه بالقدح في إمامة الآخرين وتقريره أنه لا نزاع في وجود إمام بعد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وغير علي من الجماعة الموسومين بذلك لا يصلح لذلك أما إجمالا فلظلمهم لسبق كفرهم لقوله تعالى والكافرون هم الظالمون والظالم لا يكون إماما لقوله تعالى لا ينال عهدي الظالمين والجواب منع المقدمتين ومنع دلالة الآية على كون من كان كافرا ثم أسلم ظالما ومنع كون المراد بالعهد هو الإمامة وإما تفصيلا فمما يقدح في إمامة أبي بكر رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه خالف كتاب الله تعالى في منع إرث النبي بخبر رواه وهو نحن معاشر الأنبياء لا نورث ما تركناه صدقة وتخصيص الكتاب إنما يجوز بالخبر المتواتر دون الآحاد والجواب أن خبر الواحد وإن كان ظني المتن قد يكون قطعي الدلالة فيخصص به عام الكتاب لكونه ظني الدلالة وإن كان قطعي المتن جمعا بين الدليلين وتمام تحقيق ذلك في أصول الفقه على أن الخبرالمسموع من فم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إن لم يكن فوق المتواتر فلا خفاء في كونه بمنزلته فيجوز للسامع المجتهد أن يخصص به عام الكتاب

title: Fadak: the allegation and the legal reply
en:
Another criticism is that he withheld Fadak—a village in Khaybar—from Fāṭima, although she claimed that the Prophet had bestowed it upon her as a gift, and ʿAlī and Umm Ayman testified to that. He did not accept their testimony, yet accepted the Prophet’s wives’ claims to their apartments without a witness. Such injustice and partiality are unbefitting an imam; hence the Marwānid ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz restored Fadak to Fāṭima’s children.
The reply is that, even granting the report’s truth, a judge is not obliged to rule on the testimony of one man and one woman, even supposing the claimant and witness infallible; and he may judge on what he knows with certainty even without a witness. By my life, the story of Fadak as the Rāfiḍa relate it is among the clearest indications of their absorption in error, their fabrications against the Companions, and their utmost waywardness and impudence: they suppose men such as Abū Bakr and ʿUmar unjustly seized the right of the Prophet’s offspring so that others—not themselves or their associates—might benefit; that a man such as ʿAlī, knowing the true situation, did not remove that injustice during his own caliphate; and that the other Companions kept silent without intervention or objection.
ar: ومنها أنه منع فاطمة رضي الله تعالى عنها فدك وهي قرية بخيبر مع أنها ادعت أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قد نحلها إياها ووهبها منها وشهد بذلك علي رضي الله تعالى عنه وأم أيمن فلم يصدقهم وصدق أزواج النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم في ادعاء الحجرة لهن من غير شاهد ومثل هذا الجور والميل لا يليق بالإمام ولهذا رد عمر بن عبد العزيز من المروانية فدك إلى أولاد فاطمة رضي الله تعالى عنها والجواب أنه لو سلم صحة ما ذكر فليس على الحاكم أن يحكم بشهادة رجل وامرأة وأن فرض عصمة المدعي والشاهد وله الحكم بما علمه يقينا وإن لم يشهد به شاهد ولعمري أن قصة فدك على ما يرويه الروافض من أبين الشواهد على أنهماكهم في الضلالة وافترائهم على الصحابة وكونهم الغاية في الغواية والنهاية في الوقاحة حيث ظنوا بمثل أبي بكر وعمر أنهما أخذا حق سلالة النبوة ظلما لينتفع به الآخرون لا هما نفسهما ولا من يتصل بهما ويمثل علي رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه مع علمه بحقيقة الحال لم يدفع تلك الظلامة أيام خلافته ولسائر الأصحاب أنهم سكتوا على ذلك من غير تعرض ولا اعتراض

en_html: Another criticism is that he withheld Fadak—a village in Khaybar—from Fāṭima, although she claimed that the Prophet had bestowed it upon her as a gift, and ʿAlī and Umm Ayman testified to that. He did not accept their testimony, yet accepted the Prophet’s wives’ claims to their apartments without a witness. Such injustice and partiality are unbefitting an imam; hence the Marwānid ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz restored Fadak to Fāṭima’s children. The reply is that, even granting the report’s truth, a judge is not obliged to rule on the testimony of one man and one woman, even supposing the claimant and witness infallible; and he may judge on what he knows with certainty even without a witness. title: The source’s account of later ownership of Fadak
en: The histories relate that Fadak remained under the arrangement established by Abū Bakr until Muʿāwiya’s time. He then granted it to Marwān b. al-Ḥakam, and Marwān gave it to his two sons, ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and ʿAbd al-Malik. When al-Walīd b. ʿAbd al-Malik took office, ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz gave al-Walīd his share, and Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik did likewise, so that it all belonged to al-Walīd. During his caliphate, ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz restored its earlier arrangement. Then, in the year 220, al-Maʾmūn wrote to his governor in Medina, Qutham b. Jaʿfar, instructing him to restore Fadak to Fāṭima’s descendants. He entrusted it to Muḥammad b. al-Ḥusayn b. Zayd b. ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn b. ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib and Muḥammad b. ʿAbd Allāh b. Zayd b. al-Ḥusayn b. Zayd, to administer it for their families. This was counted among al-Maʾmūn’s Shīʿī inclinations. When al-Mutawakkil became caliph, he restored the previous arrangement.
ar: والمذكور في كتب التواريخ أن فدك كانت على ما قرره أبو بكر رضي الله تعالى عنه إلى زمن معاوية ثم اقطعها مروان بن الحكم ووهبها مروان من ابنيه عبدالعزيز وعبدالملك ثم لما ولى الوليد بن عبدالملك وهب عمر بن عبدالعزيز نصيبه للوليد وكذا سليمان بن عبدالملك فصارت كلها للوليد ثم ردها عمر بن عبدالعزيز أيام خلافته إلى ما كانت عليه ثم لما كانت سنة عشرين ومائتين كتب المأمون إلى عامله على المدينة فثم بن جعفر أن يرد فدك إلى أولاد فاطمة رضي الله تعالى عنها فدفعها إلى محمد بن الحسين بن زيد بن علي بن الحسين ابن علي بن أبي طالب ومحمد بن عبد الله ابن زيد بن الحسين بن زيد ليقوما بها لأهلهما وعد ذلك من تشيع المأمون فلما استخلف المتوكل ردها إلى ما كانت عليه

title: The objection to Abū Bakr’s appointment of ʿUmar
en:
Another criticism is that he opposed the Messenger concerning succession by appointing ʿUmar as his successor. The Messenger, though better acquainted with benefits and harms and more compassionate toward the community, appointed no successor; indeed, he dismissed ʿUmar after entrusting him with the alms. Appointing him as successor and placing all Muslim affairs in his charge therefore opposes the Messenger and abandons the required following of him.
We reply: we do not concede that he appointed no successor; rather, it is agreed that he appointed one—Abū Bakr according to us and ʿAlī according to you. Nor do we concede that he dismissed ʿUmar: his commission ended when its task ended, just as someone commissioned for a job ceases to hold it upon completion; this is not dismissal. Nor do we concede that merely doing something the Prophet did not do opposes him or abandons his example. That occurs only by doing what he forbade or omitting what he commanded. Nor do we concede that the alleged act compromises entitlement to the imamate.
ar: ومنها أنه خالف رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في الاستخلاف حيث جعل عمر خليفة له والرسول عليه الصلاة والسلام مع أنه أعرف بالمصالح والمفاسد وأوفر شفقة على الأمة لم يستخلف أحدا بل عزل عمر بعد ما ولاه أمر الصدقات فاستخلافه وتوليته جميع أمور المسلمين مخالفة للرسول وترك لما وجب من اتباعه والجواب أنا لا نسلم انه لم يستخلف أحدا بل استخلف إجماعا أما عندنا فأبا بكر وأما عندكم فعليا ولا نسلم أنه عزل عمر بل انقضى توليته بانقضاء شغله كماإذا وليت أحدا عملا فأتمه فلم يبق عاملا فإنه ليس من العزل في شيء ولا نسلم أن مجرد فعل مالم يفعله النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مخالفة له وترك لاتباعه وإنما يكون ذلك إذا فعل ما نهى عنه أو ترك ما أمر به ولا نسلم أن هذا قادح في استحقاق الإمامة

title: Legal knowledge, uncertainty, and the abrupt pledge
en:
Another criticism is that he did not know the rulings: he cut off a thief’s left hand at the wrist rather than the right; and when a grandmother asked about her inheritance, he said, “I find nothing for you in God’s Book or His Prophet’s practice,” until al-Mughīra and Muḥammad b. Salama informed him that the Messenger had given her a sixth and said, “Give grandmothers a sixth.” He also did not know kalāla: one without a parent or child, or any heir who is neither a parent nor a child. Even granting these reports, the reply is that this does not invalidate his competence for juristic reasoning; how many similar cases occur among qualified jurists!
Another criticism is that, at death, he doubted his entitlement to the imamate, saying, “I wish I had asked the Messenger to whom this office belongs, so that we would not dispute it with those entitled to it.” Assuming the report sound, it indicates not doubt but the absence of an explicit designation, that his imamate rested on allegiance and selection, and that his pursuit of truth led him not to be satisfied with those alone but to desire to follow an explicit designation in particular.
Another criticism is that ʿUmar, although his ally and supporter, said, “Abū Bakr’s pledge was an abrupt affair whose evil God averted; whoever returns to its like, kill him”—meaning that it was sudden, without reflection or a foundation. The reply is that it means an unexpected occurrence from which God averted the disagreement that nearly arose; whoever returns to a division of that kind, scattering the community’s unity, is the one threatened. How could ʿUmar attack Abū Bakr’s imamate, given his well-known insistence upon honouring him and securing allegiance to him, and his own becoming caliph through Abū Bakr’s designation? They have many stories of this kind, most fabricated; even so, these admit of explanations and interpretations, and cannot outweigh the mutual affection established by the narratives and recurrently known among the community. How ugly it is to build a doctrine upon absurdities and invented reports!

unit_notes: Kalāla is a technical inheritance term. The forms «محمد بن سلمة», «لم تعرف», and «وفي الله» are preserved in Arabic; contextual English reads a male subject and the sense waqā (“averted”). The violent wording is a report discussed in a medieval argument, not an instruction from this edition. The precise wording and attribution of each report remain to be checked.
en_html: Another criticism is that he did not know the rulings: he cut off a thief’s left hand at the wrist rather than the right; and when a grandmother asked about her inheritance, he said, “I find nothing for you in God’s Book or His Prophet’s practice,” until al-Mughīra and Muḥammad b. Salama informed him that the Messenger had given her a sixth and said, “Give grandmothers a sixth.” He also did not know kalāla: one without a parent or child, or any heir who is neither a parent nor a child. Even granting these reports, the reply is that this does not invalidate his competence for juristic reasoning; how many similar cases occur among qualified jurists! Another criticism is that, at death, he doubted his entitlement to the imamate, saying, “I wish I had asked the Messenger to whom this office belongs, so that we would not dispute it with those entitled to it.” Assuming the report sound, it indicates not doubt but the absence of an explicit designation, that his imamate rested on allegiance and selection, and that his pursuit of truth led him not to be satisfied with those alone but to desire to follow an explicit designation in particular. Another criticism is that ʿUmar, although his ally and supporter, said, “Abū Bakr’s pledge was an abrupt affair whose evil God averted; whoever returns to its like, kill him”—meaning that it was sudden, without reflection or a foundation. The reply is that it means an unexpected occurrence from which God averted the disagreement that nearly arose; whoever returns to a division of that kind, scattering the community’s unity, is the one threatened. How could ʿUmar attack Abū Bakr’s imamate, given his well-known insistence upon honouring him and securing allegiance to him, and his own becoming caliph through Abū Bakr’s designation? They have many stories of this kind, most fabricated; even so, these admit of explanations and interpretations, and cannot outweigh the mutual affection established by the narratives and recurrently known among the community. How ugly it is to build a doctrine upon absurdities and invented reports!

title: Objections concerning ʿUmar’s legal knowledge
en:
He says: as for ʿUmar’s case, they criticise his imamate on several grounds. One is that he did not know the rulings, to the point of ordering the stoning of a pregnant woman who confessed to adultery and of a woman who committed adultery while insane. ʿAlī forbade this, whereupon ʿUmar said, “Were it not for ʿAlī, ʿUmar would have perished.” He also forbade excessive marriage payments. A woman stood up and said, “Has God not said, ‘Though you have given one of them a great treasure’?” He answered, “Everyone has more understanding of the law than ʿUmar—even the secluded women.”
The reply is that, even granting the story, his knowledge of the pregnancy and insanity, and that his prohibition was intended as a legal prohibition, error in one question or more does not negate competence for juristic reasoning or invalidate the imamate. Acknowledging a deficiency is self-abasement and an indication of excellence.
ar: قال وأمر عمر قدحوا في إمامة عمر بوجوه منها أنه لم يكن عارفا بالأحكام حتى أمر برجم امرأة حامل أقرت بالزنا ورجم امرأة مجنونة زنت فنهاه علي رضي الله تعالى عنه عن ذلك فقال لولا علي لهلك عمر ونهى عن المغالاة في الصداق فقامت إليه امرأة فقالت ألم يقل الله تعالى وآتيتم إحداهن قنطارا فقال كل الناس أفقه من عمر حتى المخدرات والجواب بعد تسليم القصة وعلمه بالحمل والجنون ونهيه على وجه التحريم أن الخطأ في مسئلة وأكثر لا ينافي الاجتهاد ولا يقدح في الإمامة والاعتراف بالنقصان هضم للنفس ودليل على الكمال

title: ʿUmar’s reaction to the Prophet’s death
en: Another criticism is that he did not know the Qurʾān: he doubted the Prophet’s death and did not accept it until Abū Bakr recited, “You will die, and they will die.” He then said, “It is as though I had not heard this verse.” The reply is that this arose from distraction, distress, and forgetfulness of evident matters. Alternatively, he understood from “He it is who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion,” and “He will surely make them successors in the land,” that the Prophet would remain until these matters were accomplished and fully manifested. His words, “As though I had not heard,” indicate that he had heard and known the verse, but had forgotten it or understood it differently: as though he had not heard it with awareness of this meaning, but had understood that the Prophet would die only after the affairs were completed.
ar: ومنها أنه لم يكن عالما بالقرآن حتى شك في موت النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ولم يسكن إليه حتى تلا عليه أبو بكر قوله إنك ميت وإنهم ميتون فقال كأني لم أسمع هذه الآية فالجواب أن ذلك كان لتشوش البال واضطراب الحال والذهول عن جليات الأحوال أو لأنه فهم من قوله تعالى هو الذي أرسل رسوله بالهدى ودين الحق ليظهره على الدين كله وقوله ليستخلفنهم في الأرض انه يبقى إلى تمام هذه الأمور وظهورها غاية الظهور وفي قوله كأني لم أسمع دلالة على أنه سمعها وعلمها لكن ذهل عنها أو حملها على معنى آخر أي كأني لم أسمعها سماع اطلاع على هذا المعنى بل أنه يموت بعد تمام الأمور

title: Treasury distributions and the share of the Prophet’s kin
en:
Another criticism is that he disposed of treasury funds without right, giving large sums to the Prophet’s wives—it is reported that he gave ʿĀʾisha and Ḥafṣa ten thousand dirhams annually and borrowed eighty thousand dirhams for himself. Likewise, in distributing booty he preferred the Emigrants to the Anṣār and Arabs to non-Arabs, and withheld from the Prophet’s household their fifth, the share belonging to near relatives by the Book’s ruling.
The reply is that anyone who follows the recurrently transmitted accounts of his conduct knows with certainty that this account of his use of funds is sheer fabrication. As for unequal allocation, he may do so according to what he judges beneficial, since it belongs to questions of juristic reasoning in which no decisive proof settles the matter. As for the fifth, it belonged by text and consensus to the near relatives, namely Banū Hāshim and Banū al-Muṭṭalib among the descendants of ʿAbd Manāf. But he reasoned that poverty was the basis of entitlement and restricted it to their poor, or that it belonged to the class of impure proceeds forbidden to Banū Hāshim. In short, this is a question of juristic reasoning, familiar in the law books, and does not invalidate entitlement to the imamate.
ar: ومنها أنه تصرف في بيت المال بغير الحق فأعطى أزواج النبي عليه السلام منه مالا كثيرا حتى روي أنه أعطى عايشة وحفصة كل سنة عشرة آلاف درهم وافترض لنفسه منه ثمانين ألف درهم وكذا في أموال الغنايم حيث فضل المهاجرين على الأنصار والعرب على العجم ومنع أهل البيت خمسهم الذي هو سهم ذوي القربى بحكم الكتاب والجواب أن من تتبع ما تواتر من أحواله علم قطعا أن حديث التصرف في الأموال محض افتراء وأما التفضيل فله ذلك بحسب ما يرى من المصلحة فإنه من الاجتهاديات التي لا قاطع فيها وأما الخمس فقد كان لذوي القربى وهم بنو هاشم وبنو المطلب من أولاد عبد مناف بالنص والإجماع إلا أنه اجتهد فذهب إلى أن مناط الاستحقاق هو الفقر فخصه بالفقراء منهم أو إلى أنها من قبيل الأوساخ المحرمة على بني هاشم وبالجملة فهذه مسئلة اجتهادية معروفة في كتب الفقه لا تقدح في استحقاق الإمامة

section: 45 · Investigation V: the succession and the first four caliphs
unit_notes: The witness reads «وافترض», contextually rendered “borrowed” as an expected «واقترض»; this is a recorded conjectural reading. The terminology of “impure proceeds” reflects the source’s legal characterisation and does not assert that all the kinds of revenue discussed are legally identical. The exact allocation of the fifth is not reconstructed beyond the passage.
en_html: Another criticism is that he disposed of treasury funds without right, giving large sums to the Prophet’s wives—it is reported that he gave ʿĀʾisha and Ḥafṣa ten thousand dirhams annually and borrowed eighty thousand dirhams for himself. Likewise, in distributing booty he preferred the Emigrants to the Anṣār and Arabs to non-Arabs, and withheld from the Prophet’s household their fifth, the share belonging to near relatives by the Book’s ruling. The reply is that anyone who follows the recurrently transmitted accounts of his conduct knows with certainty that this account of his use of funds is sheer fabrication. As for unequal allocation, he may do so according to what he judges beneficial, since it belongs to questions of juristic reasoning in which no decisive proof settles the matter. As for the fifth, it belonged by text and consensus to the near relatives, namely Banū Hāshim and Banū al-Muṭṭalib among the descendants of ʿAbd Manāf. But he reasoned that poverty was the basis of entitlement and restricted it to their poor, or that it belonged to the class of impure proceeds forbidden to Banū Hāshim. In short, this is a question of juristic reasoning, familiar in the law books, and does not invalidate entitlement to the imamate.

title: The two mutʿas: definitions, objection, and answer
en:
Another criticism is that he prohibited temporary marriage, mutʿat al-nikāḥ: saying to a woman, “I shall enjoy union with you for such a period for such a number of dirhams,” or “Grant me union with yourself for so many days for such a payment,” or words of that meaning. Mālik and the Shīʿa permitted it. Marriage for a specified term is of the same import; Zufar permitted it as a binding marriage. He also prohibited the pilgrimage form of tamattuʿ: a person living at a distance from Mecca which permits shortening the prayer enters consecration, performs the lesser pilgrimage in the pilgrimage months, remains in Mecca outside consecration, and commences the major pilgrimage from there in the same year. Yet he acknowledged the lawful status of both practices in the Prophet’s time, as in the report that he said: “Three things existed in the Messenger’s time which I prohibit and declare unlawful: temporary union with women, tamattuʿ in pilgrimage, and ‘Come to the best of works.’”
The reply is that these are questions of juristic reasoning. The abrogation of the permission for temporary union with women has been established by well-known reports and the Companions’ consensus. Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya reports from ʿAlī that the Messenger’s herald proclaimed on the day of Khaybar, “God and His Messenger forbid you temporary marriage.” Jābir b. Zayd said that Ibn ʿAbbās did not leave this world before retracting his views on currency exchange and temporary marriage. Some hold that its permission was established only for a temporary period of three days. “I declare them unlawful” means “I judge them unlawful and believe this on the basis of the evidence,” just as one says that al-Shāfiʿī prohibited wine reduced to a third and Abū Ḥanīfa permitted it.
ar: ومنها أنه منع متعة النكاح وهي أن يقول لامرأة تمتع بك كذا مدة بكذا درهما أو متعيني نفسك أياما بكذا أو ما يؤدى هذا المعنى وجوزها مالك والشيعة وفي معناها النكاح إلى أجل معلوم وجوزه زفر لازما ومتعة الحج وهي أن يأتي مكة من على مسافة لقصر منها محرما فيعتمر في أشهر الحج ويقيم حلالا بمكة وينشئ منها الحج عامه ذلك وقد كان معترفا بشرعية المتعتين في عهد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم على ما روي عنه أنه قال ثلاث كن على عهد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنا أنهى عنهن وأحرمهن وهي متعة النساء ومتعة الحج وحي على خير العمل والجواب أن هذه مسائل اجتهادية وقد ثبت نسخ إباحة متعة النساء بالآثار المشهورة إجماعا من الصحابة على ما روى محمد بن الحنفية عن علي رضي الله تعالى عنه أن منادي رسول الله نادى يوم خيبر ألا إن الله ورسوله ينهيانكم عن المتعة وقال جابر بن زيد ما خرج ابن عباس من الدنيا حتى رجع عن قوله في الصرف والمتعة وبعضهم على أنه إنما تثبت إباحتها موقتة بثلاثة أيام ومعنى أحرمهن أحكم بحرمتهن وأعتقد ذلك لقيام الدليل كما يقال حرم المثلث الشافعي رضي الله تعالى عنه وأباحه أبو حنيفة رحمه الله تعالى

unit_notes: The attribution to Mālik is the witness’s wording and requires independent checking; it is not silently corrected or presented as a verified account of his school. Muthallath denotes a drink reduced by boiling to a third; the English wording identifies the legal object without endorsing the ruling. “Come to the best of works” is the disputed call-to-prayer formula. This is translation of historical debate, not present-day marital, pilgrimage, or alcohol guidance.
